newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian firms 96/97 results worst in 10 years - CMIE.
newsitem.headline: Indian firms 96/97 results worst in 10 years - CMIE.

text.p: Indian firms recorded a sharp decline in profits during the year that ended March 31, the Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy (CMIE) said on Monday.
"The performance is the worst recorded by the corporate sector in the past 10 years," the independent think-tank said.
CMIE said it had studied the preliminary results of over 500 non-finance firms.
It said Indian firms have been recording almost 20 percent nominal sales growth between 1987/88 and 1995/96. In recent years -- 1994/95 and 1995/96, the growth rate averaged 25 percent a year.
"The accelerating pace of sales expansion was severed to half as the sales growth in 1996/97 was barely 11 percent," CMIE said in its Monthly Review of the Indian Economy for May.
In real terms, the growth is estimated at about 7.0 percent.
More than 200 companies, constituting over 35 percent of the sample, recorded a decline in sales, CMIE said. Small companies recorded a sharp fall in sales.
Several pharmaceutical firms recorded healthy sales growth rates. Ranbaxy Laboratories recorded a 22 percent rie, Dabur 26 percent, Cipla 25 percent and Orchid Chemicals 72 percent, CMIE said.
Gujarat Narmada Valley Fertilizers sales grew 52 percent and that of Larsen & Toubro by 25 percent.
Indo Gulf Fertilisers, SuRaj Diamonds, SIV Industries are among the companies which recorded a fall in sales during 1996/97, it said.
CMIE said profit after tax of the non-finance private sector companies fell by over six percent in 1996/97.
"This is the first time, at least in the past one decade, that the Indian corporate sector recorded a decline," it said.

The growth in profit after tax over the last decade has been volatile -- oscillating from single digit growth rates to nearly 90 percent. "However, never did the growth halt. In 1996/97, it did to fall a full 10 percent," it added.
CMIE said the overall 10 percent fall in profit after tax does not reflect the profit growth of sample firms.

"Over 54 percent of the companies recorded a decline in profit after tax. Nearly half of these recorded a decline of close to or over 50 percent. On the other hand, nearly 20 percent of the comanies recorded a 50 percent or more growth in profit after tax during the year," CMIE said.
Reliance Industries, Larsen & Toubro and Bajaj Auto recorded nominal increases in profit after tax but most other large firms recorded a fall, it said.
The share of depreciation provision rose to 19 percent in 1996/97 from 17 percent a year ago, CMIE said.
"With the introduction of MAT (minimum alternate tax), many companies have changed their depreciation provisioning methods to report higher depreciation and lesser book profits."
The share of corporate taxes also increased marginally thanks to MAT, CMIE said.
